planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after all danger of frost in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; indoors or in hanging baskets it can be planted year-round.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade, where the thin, lance-shaped leaves striped in white, pink, and green will trail and root readily wherever nodes touch soil. Pinch stem tips periodically to keep the mounding, cascading habit dense rather than leggy. North of zone 9 it is grown as a shade annual, hanging-basket trailer, or houseplant and is killed outright by frost. Keep out of direct sun, which scorches the thin variegated foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade in spring; this woodland-edge grass resents heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: Plant small divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge or under high, open canopy where some filtered sun reaches the ground. Mountain melick forms neat, low tufts of narrow green leaves and sends up slender, arching stems hung with small, one-sided, nodding purplish-brown spikelets in late spring that sway attractively in the lightest breeze. It is slow to spread and never aggressive, making it suitable for small woodland rock gardens or beneath deciduous shrubs. Established clumps need little supplemental water once rooted and resent soggy winter soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; unlike most ornamental fescues it genuinely needs shelter from direct sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil beneath beech or oak canopy or in any cool, shaded border, where wood fescue's broad, soft, glossy dark-green blades form a lax, fountain-like clump quite unlike the stiff blue needle-leaved fescues grown for sun. Loose, airy flower panicles rise well above the foliage in early to midsummer on wiry stems. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form an attractive, dense colony and tolerates deeper shade than almost any other fescue. Avoid hot, dry, or exposed sites, which cause the foliage to brown and thin.

planting.note: Direct sow in early autumn into prepared soil under tree canopy or in deep shade where turf grasses normally fail; can also be spring-sown.

directions: Broadcast seed thinly over lightly raked soil in deep woodland shade, where this fine-leaved, soft-textured bluegrass tolerates root competition and low light better than almost any turf species, making it a mainstay of European shade-lawn seed blends. Left unmown it forms loose, airy tufts topped by delicate, open flower panicles in late spring. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes and self-seeds modestly, filling in bare, shaded patches under mature trees where fescues and bluegrasses bred for sun struggle. Mow high, if mowing at all, to keep plants vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, fertile soil in partial to full shade in spring; this woodland grass thrives on humus-rich ground under deciduous trees.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where the unusually broad, glossy, pleated leaf blades set this grass apart from the narrow-leaved meadow grasses typical of open lawns. Loose, open flower panicles appear above the foliage clump in early summer on upright stems. It forms a slowly expanding tuft rather than running aggressively, so it combines well with shade perennials in a woodland border without overwhelming neighbors. Division every few years in spring keeps clumps vigorous and prevents the centers from thinning.
